disclaimer: ILLUSTRATIVE MOCK DATA. Organisation and individual names are real and used for realism, but every relationship state, trajectory, strength score, exposure figure, event and narrative in this file is invented for a technical assignment. Nothing here is reporting, and none of it should be read as a factual claim about any real entity or person.

nodes.name: Repsol
nodes.role: Client — Spanish integrated energy company
nodes.description: Integrated oil, gas and increasingly electricity company headquartered in Madrid, with upstream positions across North Africa and the Americas and a large Iberian downstream and retail footprint. Its exposure profile is unusually relationship-driven: a small number of sovereign and state-owned counterparties account for a disproportionate share of supply and production risk.

nodes.name: Government of Spain
nodes.role: Home sovereign — fiscal, energy and industrial policy
nodes.description: Sets the fiscal and permitting environment Repsol operates in, and is the ultimate arbiter of windfall levies, refinery transition timelines and hydrogen subsidy allocation. Also the diplomatic channel through which the Algeria supply relationship is mediated.

nodes.name: Government of Algeria
nodes.role: Host state — controls the single largest gas supply channel
nodes.description: Controls Sonatrach and therefore the pricing and reliability of the Medgaz-routed gas that underpins a large share of Iberian supply. Political relations with Madrid have been the dominant swing factor in Repsol's supply cost base since 2022.

nodes.name: Government of Venezuela
nodes.role: Host state — sanctioned production and unresolved arrears
nodes.description: Hosts joint-venture production that has been intermittently accessible depending on the prevailing US licensing regime. The state is simultaneously partner, debtor and expropriation risk, which makes this the most volatile single relationship in the portfolio.

nodes.name: Government of Libya
nodes.role: Host state — fragmented authority over producing assets
nodes.description: Authority over the producing concessions is contested between rival administrations, so contractual counterparty risk is less about policy direction than about which body is recognised at any given moment. Production has repeatedly been interrupted by force majeure at the terminal level.

nodes.name: Government of Mexico
nodes.role: Host state — upstream licensing and Pemex primacy
nodes.description: Controls the licensing round framework under which foreign upstream participation operates, and has consistently prioritised Pemex in the allocation of new acreage. Policy direction determines whether existing discoveries can be developed on commercial terms.

nodes.name: Government of the United States
nodes.role: Extraterritorial regulator via sanctions and licensing
nodes.description: Not a host state for material production, but the single most consequential external actor because its licensing decisions determine whether Venezuelan barrels can legally be lifted and monetised. Its posture can change the value of an entire asset overnight without any action by Repsol.

nodes.name: European Commission
nodes.role: Supranational regulator — emissions, taxonomy, state aid
nodes.description: Sets the emissions trading cost curve, the sustainable-finance taxonomy that governs how Repsol's transition capex is classified, and the state-aid rules constraining Spanish hydrogen support. Directionally the most important regulator for the 2030 business model.

nodes.name: CNMC
nodes.role: Spanish markets and competition authority
nodes.description: Supervises fuel retail pricing and competitive conduct in the Iberian downstream market, and reviews consolidation in electricity retail. Its enforcement posture is the main constraint on margin capture in the domestic service-station network.

nodes.name: MITECO
nodes.role: Spanish ministry for ecological transition
nodes.description: Owns the permitting pipeline for renewables build-out and the refinery decarbonisation timetable. Effectively decides the speed at which Repsol can convert legacy refining assets into low-carbon fuel production.

nodes.name: US OFAC
nodes.role: US Treasury sanctions administrator
nodes.description: Issues and revokes the specific licences that permit oil-for-debt recovery in Venezuela. Repsol has no relationship leverage here at all — the exposure is entirely one-directional and the notice period on changes is effectively zero.

nodes.name: Sonatrach
nodes.role: Algerian national oil and gas company
nodes.description: Counterparty on long-term gas supply contracts and a partner in Algerian upstream acreage. Contract pricing has been reopened repeatedly since 2022, and the commercial relationship is now effectively an extension of the Madrid–Algiers political relationship.

nodes.name: PDVSA
nodes.role: Venezuelan state oil company and JV partner
nodes.description: Joint-venture partner in producing assets and the entity against which historical receivables are held. Repayment has been structured in barrels rather than cash, which ties recovery of the outstanding balance directly to the US licensing position.

nodes.name: National Oil Corporation (Libya)
nodes.role: Libyan state oil company and concession counterparty
nodes.description: Nominal counterparty for Libyan production regardless of which political authority is ascendant, which has given it unusual institutional continuity. Operational reliability is nonetheless governed by local security conditions rather than by contract.

nodes.name: Pemex
nodes.role: Mexican state oil company — partner and gatekeeper
nodes.description: Both a joint-venture partner on discovered resources and the favoured national champion competing for the same acreage. Its financial condition is a live counterparty risk on any shared development commitment.

nodes.name: TotalEnergies
nodes.role: Consortium partner upstream — competitor downstream
nodes.description: Sits on the same side of the table in North African producing consortia and on the opposite side in European retail and low-carbon fuels. This dual role is structurally useful — shared operational exposure creates a channel that survives commercial rivalry.

nodes.name: OMV
nodes.role: Consortium partner in North African upstream
nodes.description: Minority consortium participant sharing operational and force-majeure exposure on the same Libyan acreage. Alignment is high because the risks are identical and neither party competes meaningfully in the other's home market.

nodes.name: Moeve (formerly Cepsa)
nodes.role: Principal Iberian downstream rival
nodes.description: The closest structural analogue to Repsol in the Spanish market — refining, retail network and a parallel green hydrogen strategy competing for the same Andalusian subsidy envelope. Competition is intense but conventional.

nodes.name: Naturgy
nodes.role: Gas rival — and co-exposed to the same Algerian supply
nodes.description: Competes directly in Iberian gas and power retail while depending on the same Algerian supply channel. That shared dependency creates occasional alignment of interest in dealings with Algiers, which is rare between direct competitors.

nodes.name: Iberdrola
nodes.role: Electricity incumbent — competitor in the transition
nodes.description: Holds the position in Spanish electricity that Repsol is attempting to build into, and has publicly argued for policy that favours pure-play renewables over integrated transition models. The rivalry is as much regulatory-lobbying as commercial.

nodes.name: BP
nodes.role: International major — competitor for assets and capital
nodes.description: Competes for the same upstream acreage and for the same pool of transition-oriented institutional capital. Its strategic reversals on transition pace directly affect how investors benchmark Repsol's own capex allocation.

nodes.name: Sacyr
nodes.role: Long-standing large domestic shareholder
nodes.description: A significant domestic shareholder whose own balance-sheet needs have historically driven its posture on dividends and board composition. The relationship is governance-critical out of proportion to the stake size because of its influence on board dynamics.

nodes.name: BlackRock
nodes.role: Major institutional shareholder
nodes.description: Index-driven holder whose stewardship positions set the tone for how the wider institutional base votes on transition disclosure and remuneration. Engagement is procedural rather than personal, but the voting outcome is material.

nodes.name: Norges Bank Investment Management
nodes.role: Sovereign wealth shareholder with an ethics mandate
nodes.description: Holds a meaningful index position under an explicit ethical exclusion framework, which makes its continued participation a public signal about Repsol's transition credibility. Divestment risk is reputational as much as financial.

nodes.name: Banco Santander
nodes.role: Relationship lender and facility arranger
nodes.description: Core domestic banking relationship providing revolving facilities and arranging syndications. Increasingly applies sustainability-linked pricing terms that couple borrowing cost to emissions performance.

nodes.name: European Investment Bank
nodes.role: Policy lender for transition projects
nodes.description: Potential concessional funding source for hydrogen and low-carbon fuel projects, but bound by lending criteria that exclude most hydrocarbon-linked activity. Access is contingent on project structure rather than on the corporate relationship.

nodes.name: Iberia
nodes.role: Flag carrier — sustainable aviation fuel offtaker
nodes.description: Anchor offtake counterparty for sustainable aviation fuel produced from converted refining capacity. The commercial value of the SAF investment case depends heavily on this class of long-dated airline commitment.

nodes.name: Maersk
nodes.role: Shipping major — low-carbon marine fuel offtaker
nodes.description: Buyer of low-carbon marine fuels under decarbonisation commitments that run ahead of regulatory requirement. A demanding counterparty on lifecycle emissions verification, which raises the compliance bar on the production side.

nodes.name: Iberian Industrial Consumers
nodes.role: Energy-intensive industrial demand base
nodes.description: Aggregate of chemicals, steel and cement offtakers whose competitiveness depends on delivered energy cost. Collectively an effective lobbying bloc on tariffs and on the pass-through of transition costs.

nodes.name: UGT-FICA
nodes.role: Industrial trade union — refining workforce
nodes.description: Represents a large share of the refining and petrochemical workforce and negotiates the sector collective agreement. Its position on refinery conversion determines whether transition milestones can be met on schedule.

nodes.name: CCOO de Industria
nodes.role: Industrial trade union — parallel representation
nodes.description: Second major union at the same sites, generally aligned with UGT-FICA on employment guarantees but more assertive on the pace of decarbonisation commitments. Coordination between the two determines industrial-action risk.

nodes.name: Greenpeace España
nodes.role: Campaigning environmental NGO
nodes.description: Sustained public campaigner against continued hydrocarbon investment and a persistent critic of transition-fuel claims. Influence runs through media framing and political pressure rather than through any direct commercial channel.

nodes.name: ClientEarth
nodes.role: Legal-strategy environmental NGO
nodes.description: Pursues litigation and regulatory complaints targeting corporate climate disclosure and advertising claims. More consequential than campaign NGOs because the mechanism is legally binding rather than reputational.

nodes.name: Josu Jon Imaz
nodes.role: Chief Executive Officer
nodes.description: Sets and publicly defends the integrated transition strategy, and is the principal interlocutor with government on refinery conversion and hydrogen policy. Personal credibility with Madrid is itself a component of the company's regulatory position.

nodes.name: Antonio Brufau
nodes.role: Chairman
nodes.description: Long-tenured chairman with deep institutional relationships across the Spanish corporate and political establishment, and the historical architect of much of the Latin American footprint. Board-level continuity runs through this relationship.

edges.exposure: Windfall levy exposure plus the entire domestic permitting pipeline

lastEvent.summary: Treasury signalled that the extraordinary energy levy would be reviewed rather than allowed to lapse.

edges.narrative: The foundational relationship, and still workable — but the terms have shifted. Fiscal pressure has made Repsol a convenient revenue source, and the company's leverage rests increasingly on its role in industrial employment rather than on political goodwill. Cooperative on transition policy, adversarial on tax.

edges.exposure: Roughly a quarter of contracted gas supply and shared Algerian upstream acreage

lastEvent.summary: Third price review since 2022 concluded with a narrower indexation gap than the previous round.

edges.narrative: The single largest supply dependency, and the one with the least contractual protection — pricing has been reopened three times in four years. The most recent review closed on better terms than expected, which suggests the worst of the repricing cycle has passed. Still structurally fragile because commercial terms track political weather in Algiers.

edges.exposure: Sovereign control over the counterparty on the largest supply contract

lastEvent.summary: Bilateral ministerial contact resumed after an extended freeze in high-level engagement.

edges.narrative: Repsol has no direct lever here; the relationship is mediated entirely through Madrid and moves with the diplomatic cycle. Recent resumption of ministerial contact is the leading indicator for the Sonatrach commercial position, which is why this edge is worth tracking separately from the contract itself.

edges.exposure: JV production plus an unrecovered receivable balance repaid in barrels

lastEvent.summary: Barrel-denominated repayment schedule slipped for the second consecutive quarter.

edges.narrative: Functional only while the licensing window stays open. Repsol needs the barrels to recover the receivable and PDVSA needs the operating capability, which keeps it transactional rather than hostile — but neither party controls the variable that actually governs it, which sits in Washington.

edges.exposure: Expropriation and contract-repudiation risk on the entire JV position

lastEvent.summary: Renewed official commentary on revising foreign participation terms in existing ventures.

edges.narrative: A relationship maintained because exit would crystallise the loss rather than because it is productive. The state is partner, debtor and principal risk simultaneously. Any deterioration in the US licensing position removes the last reason for Caracas to preserve the arrangement.

edges.exposure: Legality of all Venezuelan lifting and debt recovery

lastEvent.summary: Specific licence renewed for a shorter term than the preceding authorisation.

edges.narrative: Zero leverage, maximum consequence — the defining asymmetric exposure in the portfolio. Repsol is a licence holder, not a counterparty, and the shortening renewal term is a deliberate signal. This edge should be read as a control on the Venezuela cluster rather than as a relationship.

edges.exposure: Policy direction governing all sanctions-linked positions

lastEvent.summary: Policy review signalled a tightening posture toward third-country operators in sanctioned jurisdictions.

edges.narrative: Distinct from the OFAC edge: this is the political current that determines what OFAC does. Repsol's influence is limited to coalition work with other European operators and to Spanish diplomatic channels. Direction of travel is unfavourable.

edges.exposure: Operated concession production subject to recurrent force majeure

lastEvent.summary: Production resumed following a terminal-level blockade lasting several weeks.

edges.narrative: Remarkably durable at the institutional level — the NOC has outlasted every political configuration around it, and the commercial relationship has survived accordingly. The risk is not the counterparty; it is the security environment, which no amount of relationship management addresses.

edges.exposure: Contested authority over concession validity

lastEvent.summary: Competing administrations issued conflicting statements on hydrocarbon revenue allocation.

edges.narrative: There is no single counterparty to have a relationship with, which is itself the finding. Repsol manages this by dealing with the NOC and staying out of the political dispute — a deliberate and, so far, effective non-engagement posture.

edges.exposure: Shared development commitments on discovered resources

lastEvent.summary: Partner cash-call timing renegotiated on a shared development.

edges.narrative: Cooperation is real but constrained by Pemex's financial condition — the partnership functions until a capital call arrives. Structurally awkward because the same entity is both partner and the favoured competitor for new acreage.

edges.exposure: Access to new licensing rounds and development approvals

lastEvent.summary: Licensing round scope again limited in favour of national-champion allocation.

edges.narrative: Not hostile, but consistently unfavourable — policy has settled into a stable equilibrium that limits foreign upside without threatening existing positions. Plan around it rather than expecting it to move.

edges.exposure: Carbon cost curve and taxonomy treatment of all transition capex

lastEvent.summary: Consultation opened on tightening the taxonomy treatment of low-carbon liquid fuels.

edges.narrative: The most consequential regulator for the 2030 business model. Repsol's integrated transition strategy depends on low-carbon fuels being classified favourably, and the current consultation runs against that. Engagement is technically sophisticated but the direction is unfavourable.

edges.exposure: Permitting velocity on renewables and refinery conversion

lastEvent.summary: Conversion milestone approved on the original timetable.

edges.narrative: The most functional regulatory relationship in the portfolio. Interests are genuinely aligned — the ministry needs industrial decarbonisation to be visibly working, and Repsol needs permits. Worth protecting, because it partially offsets the Commission's direction of travel.

edges.exposure: Retail fuel margin and electricity retail consolidation approvals

lastEvent.summary: Market monitoring extended to cover fuel retail pricing behaviour more closely.

edges.narrative: Correct and procedural, with no reservoir of goodwill in either direction. Increased monitoring of retail pricing is the practical constraint on domestic margin, and the posture has hardened over the past year.

edges.exposure: Shared consortium interests in North African producing acreage

lastEvent.summary: Consortium partners coordinated a joint response to a production interruption.

edges.narrative: Genuinely aligned where the exposure is shared. Identical force-majeure risk produces real operational cooperation, and this channel has proved durable even while the two compete hard elsewhere.

edges.exposure: Competing positions in European retail and low-carbon fuels

lastEvent.summary: Both parties bid competing low-carbon fuel projects into the same EU funding call.

edges.narrative: The second edge to the same counterparty, and deliberately modelled separately. Partner upstream, rival downstream — collapsing these into one relationship would average away both signals. Competitive intensity is rising as transition subsidy pools become the contested resource.

edges.exposure: Minority consortium alignment on Libyan acreage

lastEvent.summary: Joined the coordinated consortium response on the Libyan production interruption.

edges.narrative: Low-friction and low-salience. Aligned interests, no competitive overlap in home markets, and no history of dispute. Useful precisely because it requires no management.

edges.exposure: Iberian refining margin and competing hydrogen subsidy claims

lastEvent.summary: Competing Andalusian hydrogen projects submitted into the same support scheme.

edges.narrative: Conventional commercial rivalry, conducted within normal bounds. The one place it becomes strategically material is subsidy allocation, where the pool is finite and the two are the principal claimants.

edges.exposure: Competing gas and power retail positions, shared Algerian supply dependency

lastEvent.summary: Both parties made parallel representations on Algerian supply terms.

edges.narrative: The most interesting competitor relationship: direct rivals in retail who share an upstream vulnerability. That shared exposure has begun to produce tacit coordination in dealings with Algiers, which is why the trajectory is improving despite the competitive baseline.

edges.exposure: Contested regulatory framing of integrated versus pure-play transition models

lastEvent.summary: Publicly opposing submissions filed on the treatment of low-carbon fuels in national policy.

edges.narrative: The rivalry that matters most, because it is fought in front of regulators rather than customers. Iberdrola benefits from a policy definition of transition that excludes liquid fuels; Repsol's strategy requires the opposite. Not reconcilable, and hardening.

edges.exposure: Competition for upstream acreage and for transition-oriented capital

lastEvent.summary: Investor commentary benchmarked the two companies' transition capex ratios directly.

edges.narrative: Distant competition with limited direct contact, but consequential through the capital markets — BP's strategic choices reset the benchmark against which Repsol's own transition spend is judged.

edges.exposure: Board influence and sustained pressure for dividend predictability

lastEvent.summary: Supported the board's proposed distribution policy at the general meeting.

edges.narrative: Unusual in that the dependency runs the other way — Sacyr's own financing has historically relied on the value and yield of this holding. That gives Repsol more room than the stake size implies, and relations have been settled since the distribution policy stabilised.

edges.exposure: Voting weight on transition disclosure and remuneration resolutions

lastEvent.summary: Voted with the board on all resolutions at the general meeting.

edges.narrative: Procedural and predictable. Influence is exercised through published stewardship policy rather than direct engagement, so the practical task is meeting a disclosure standard rather than managing a relationship.

edges.exposure: Reputational signal attached to continued inclusion under an ethics mandate

lastEvent.summary: Ethics council widened its review of hydrocarbon holdings.

edges.narrative: The financial stake matters less than the signal. An exclusion decision would be read by the wider ESG-constrained investor base as a verdict, and the current review widens that risk. Low probability, high consequence.

edges.exposure: Revolving credit capacity and syndication access

lastEvent.summary: Revolving facility renewed with sustainability-linked pricing terms attached.

edges.narrative: A settled domestic banking relationship on both sides. The sustainability-linked pricing is the one live variable — it converts emissions performance directly into cost of capital, which quietly aligns the lender with the NGO critique.

edges.exposure: Access to concessional funding for hydrogen and low-carbon fuel projects

lastEvent.summary: A ring-fenced hydrogen project was advanced to due diligence.

edges.narrative: Currently marginal but structurally important — concessional funding materially changes the hydrogen investment case. Access depends on ring-fencing project structures away from the hydrocarbon balance sheet, and the first test of that is now underway.

edges.exposure: Long-dated sustainable aviation fuel offtake underpinning conversion capex

lastEvent.summary: Offtake volumes extended ahead of the mandated compliance step-up.

edges.narrative: One of the few clearly improving relationships. Regulatory mandates make the airline the dependent party, and that dependency strengthens each year as blending requirements rise. This is the demand-side anchor for the whole conversion strategy.

edges.exposure: Low-carbon marine fuel offtake with lifecycle verification conditions

lastEvent.summary: Agreed a stricter lifecycle emissions verification protocol for delivered volumes.

edges.narrative: A demanding customer, and useful for exactly that reason — the verification standard it imposes is more stringent than regulation requires, which builds defensible credibility against greenwashing challenges elsewhere in the graph.

edges.exposure: Bulk industrial energy demand and joint positioning on tariff policy

lastEvent.summary: Joint industry submission opposing transition cost pass-through to industrial tariffs.

edges.narrative: Commercially routine but politically useful. When Repsol and its industrial customers align on tariff policy, the combined employment argument carries real weight in Madrid — a rare instance of a customer relationship producing regulatory leverage.

edges.exposure: Refinery conversion timetable and associated headcount commitments

lastEvent.summary: Sector agreement talks opened with employment guarantees as the lead demand.

edges.narrative: Historically constructive, and now under strain for structural rather than personal reasons: conversion reduces headcount and no amount of goodwill changes that arithmetic. The union is not opposed to transition, only to bearing its cost. Watch this edge — it gates the timetable.

edges.exposure: Parallel representation at the same sites; industrial action risk

lastEvent.summary: Joined the sector agreement talks with a firmer position on conversion pace.

edges.narrative: The more assertive of the two unions. The operative risk is not either union individually but the two coordinating — joint action would halt conversion work outright. Currently aligned on demands but not on tactics.

edges.exposure: Sustained public challenge to transition-fuel messaging

lastEvent.summary: Published a critique of low-carbon fuel emissions claims.

edges.narrative: Openly adversarial and stably so — there is no version of Repsol's strategy this actor endorses, so the relationship is managed rather than improved. Reputational rather than operational impact, and largely priced in.

edges.exposure: Litigation and regulatory complaint risk on disclosure and advertising claims

lastEvent.summary: Filed a regulatory complaint concerning low-carbon fuel advertising claims.

edges.narrative: More dangerous than the campaign NGOs because the mechanism is legal rather than reputational — an adverse ruling would bind. The complaint targets precisely the claims the transition strategy depends on communicating. Rising, and materially so.

edges.exposure: Personal credibility with Madrid as a component of regulatory standing

lastEvent.summary: Led the company's position in refinery conversion discussions with the ministry.

edges.narrative: Modelled as a node because the access is personal, not institutional — a change here would measurably weaken the MITECO channel. Key-person concentration is itself the risk being tracked.

edges.exposure: Board continuity and establishment relationships across Iberia and Latin America

lastEvent.summary: Chaired the annual general meeting.

edges.narrative: The historical relationship architecture of the Latin American footprint runs through this chair. Institutionally stable, but the long tenure makes eventual succession a live governance question that shareholders track.

edges.exposure: Full state ownership and direct control of commercial policy

lastEvent.summary: Ministry directed the terms of the concluded contract price review.

edges.narrative: The reason the Sonatrach contract cannot be treated as a purely commercial relationship. Sonatrach has no independent commercial policy, so counterparty analysis here is really sovereign analysis.

edges.exposure: The diplomatic channel that sets the tone for all Iberian gas supply

lastEvent.summary: High-level bilateral engagement resumed after a prolonged freeze.

edges.narrative: The upstream cause of Repsol's largest supply risk. This edge moves first; the Sonatrach commercial terms follow it with a lag of roughly two quarters. Treat it as the leading indicator for the whole North African cluster.

edges.exposure: Direct policy control over the licensing regime

lastEvent.summary: Policy review translated into a shorter licence renewal term.

edges.narrative: Modelled explicitly so the Venezuela exposure traces back to its actual origin. Administrative action at OFAC is downstream of political direction, and the transmission is fast.

edges.exposure: Designation status determining whether the counterparty can transact at all

lastEvent.summary: Authorisations narrowed at the latest renewal.

edges.narrative: The constraint that actually governs Repsol's Venezuelan position. Repsol's JV partner is a designated entity, so every commercial decision routes through a licence Repsol does not control.

edges.exposure: State ownership and direct control of the JV counterparty

lastEvent.summary: State reiterated its intent to review foreign participation terms.

edges.narrative: Same structural pattern as Algeria–Sonatrach: no commercial autonomy, so the partner-risk assessment collapses into sovereign risk.

edges.exposure: State ownership plus preferential acreage allocation

lastEvent.summary: Licensing scope again narrowed in the national champion's favour.

edges.narrative: Explains why Repsol's Mexican partner is also its main obstacle. The state's industrial policy and its ownership of the JV partner are the same fact.

edges.exposure: Contested political authority over the state oil company

lastEvent.summary: Rival administrations issued conflicting revenue allocation directives.

edges.narrative: The NOC's partial insulation from the political dispute is what has kept Repsol's Libyan production contractually viable. If that insulation fails, the concession position becomes genuinely uncertain.

edges.exposure: State aid approval governing national hydrogen and transition support

lastEvent.summary: National hydrogen support scheme cleared state aid review.

edges.narrative: Why MITECO's cooperative posture has a ceiling: Madrid can only support Repsol's transition to the extent Brussels permits. Constrains the most functional relationship in the portfolio.

edges.exposure: Ministerial direction over the permitting and conversion agenda

lastEvent.summary: Government reaffirmed the industrial decarbonisation timetable.

edges.narrative: Included so the reader can see that the MITECO channel is only as durable as the current government's industrial policy. Political change here propagates straight through to permitting velocity.

edges.exposure: Statutory mandate and appointments to the competition authority

lastEvent.summary: Routine appointment cycle completed.

edges.narrative: Formally independent, politically appointed. Worth surfacing because a harder consumer-price posture in Madrid tends to show up as tighter retail monitoring a few months later.

edges.exposure: Financing secured against the Repsol shareholding

lastEvent.summary: Facilities linked to the holding were refinanced.

edges.narrative: The mechanism behind Sacyr's dividend sensitivity. A financing structure resting on the stake means the shareholder's posture on distributions is driven by its own lenders, not by a view on strategy.

edges.exposure: Regulatory complaints channelled into the taxonomy consultation process

lastEvent.summary: Submitted evidence to the low-carbon fuels taxonomy consultation.

edges.narrative: The transmission mechanism that makes ClientEarth genuinely consequential. NGO pressure converts into binding regulation via the Commission — the two adverse edges in this graph are connected, and reinforcing.

edges.exposure: Coordinated campaign and litigation targeting on fuel claims

lastEvent.summary: Campaign publication and regulatory complaint landed within weeks of each other.

edges.narrative: Public campaigning builds the evidentiary and political context that litigation then exploits. Sequencing suggests coordination, which raises the effective threat level of both.

edges.exposure: Parallel long-term Algerian gas supply contracts

lastEvent.summary: Ran its own price review process on a similar timetable.

edges.narrative: The shared dependency that makes Repsol's competitor situationally an ally. Both face the same counterparty on the same terms, which is why their Algiers positions have converged.

edges.exposure: Lobbying position on the definition of qualifying transition activity

lastEvent.summary: Filed a submission favouring electrification-led classification criteria.

edges.narrative: Shows where the competitive fight is actually taking place. Iberdrola is working the same consultation that threatens Repsol's fuel classification — the rivalry and the regulatory risk are one problem, not two.

edges.exposure: Degree of coordination determines industrial action risk

lastEvent.summary: Entered sector talks with a jointly agreed set of employment demands.

edges.narrative: The edge to watch on the labour side. Individually each union is manageable; jointly they can stop conversion work. Convergence is the risk indicator, and it is currently rising.

edges.exposure: Parallel concession exposure in the same producing acreage

lastEvent.summary: Affected by the same terminal blockade as its consortium partners.

edges.narrative: Included to show that Repsol's Libyan risk is shared rather than idiosyncratic. Common exposure is what sustains consortium cooperation through interruptions.

edges.exposure: Direct ministerial access on conversion and hydrogen policy

lastEvent.summary: Represented the company directly in ministerial discussions.

edges.narrative: The personal channel underpinning the institutional relationship. Modelling it separately makes the key-person dependency visible instead of hiding it inside a corporate edge.

edges.exposure: Board-level relationship management with the largest domestic shareholder

lastEvent.summary: Shareholder supported board proposals at the general meeting.

edges.narrative: Long-standing establishment ties are the reason the shareholder relationship has stayed settled. A succession at the chair would remove that shock absorber.
